1:
Where this woe belongs turns on the chapter division. Charles Ellicott calls that division misleading: these four verses continue the preceding discourse and end with its tolling refrain, while a new section begins at the fifth verse and runs on for two chapters, the first in the collection dealing exclusively with Assyria. Matthew Henry leaves the point open but draws out what hangs on it: if the princes of Israel are meant, these verses join the previous chapter, which the repeated refrain makes probable; if those of Judah, they show why God brought the Assyrian army, to punish magistrates for a maladministration no one could call them to account for by law. John Gill raises a smaller doubt, whether the opening word is a threat denounced, as the ancient versions took it, or a vocative summons, as the Jewish grammarians read it.

The oppression they agree on. Gill has laws that discouraged the poor from applying for justice, and vexatious and expensive suits that wore them out when they did, the cause going generally for the rich. Keil and Delitzsch put it more sharply: poor men who wanted to begin proceedings were not even allowed to, and property to which widows and orphans had a well-founded claim was welcome booty. John Calvin says they were robbed for the rich and went away mocked from the judgment-seat, and explains why this class is named: the destitute lack help, and though magistrates owe them more assistance than others they take greater liberty in oppressing them.

The questions that follow are irony to one and warning to another. Ellicott hears a touch of it: had those corrupt judges asked themselves what they would do when the Supreme Judge called them to account, whether they had an ally who could protect them, a hiding-place for the treasures they had made their glory? Delitzsch notes that the word for visitation always means a visitation of punishment, and that the word for desolation is a dull confused rumbling, said to come from afar because a distant nation was the instrument. Calvin turns on the men rather than the words, princes careless and indolent in their distresses as men intoxicated by prosperity despise danger; having beaten their neighbours and allied with a great power they had ceased to fear, and he insists that though God delays he has fixed the time and it is near. Wesley identifies the far country as Assyria, and accounts for the security of a people in amity with the Assyrians next door.

The closing verse is obscure, and each takes its particle differently. Adam Clarke renders it without my aid, so that they are taken captive by the captives and subdued by the vanquished, and draws the moral that as they had lived without God in worship and obedience they should now be without his help. Wesley says the same more briefly, without the favour and help they had forfeited. Gill lists the options without choosing: forsaken by God and so bowing down, or bowing because they are not his people, or, on a rabbinic reading, the word meaning besides, so that beyond the subjection suffered at home a greater affliction is coming in captivity. Calvin gives two readings and prefers neither outright, the exclusive sense that all will be given up to captivity or death, and the causal sense that their ruin comes of revolting from God; on the second he remarks that the words become an ironical reproof of the ungodly, who boast of being forsaken as though nothing were more desirable than to withdraw as far from God as possible. Ellicott grants the text is obscure but reads it as the answer to the taunting questions, the prophet dropping the direct address for an ominous aside: no ally and no hiding-place, only bowing among the captives or falling among the slain, exile or death.
5:
The word opening this verse is read three ways, and the choice decides the tone of all that follows. John Gill lists them: a call summoning the Assyrian against the land; a sigh that God must use such an instrument against his own people; or a threat of ruin, since the ancient versions render the word as woe, in which case the verse begins the comfort rather than the sentence. John Calvin works through the same range and changes his mind in the open. The particle is sometimes lamentation, sometimes address, sometimes a woe; his first thought is that God assumes the character of one who sighs at having to punish his people so, but on closer examination he prefers the summons, God arming the Assyrians with his authority as a judge calls an officer to chain a malefactor or hands him to the executioner. John Wesley takes it as an invitation to take the charge and set about the work.

Where the section begins is agreed; its date is not. Adam Clarke calls this a new and distinct prophecy running to the end of the twelfth chapter, and dates it between Hezekiah's sixth year, when Samaria fell, and his fourteenth, since it foretells the invasion that came then. Charles Ellicott makes the same division, noting that Assyria had been mentioned before but that this is the first utterance of which it is the direct subject, so one might call it the burden of Assyria.

Ellicott supplies the history from the monuments. Some years had passed since that alliance; Damascus had been taken and Samaria reduced, and two kings had met there to do homage to their common overlord. A new king took the Assyrian throne, began the conquest of Samaria and carried off the ten tribes, and on his death the throne was seized by his own commander-in-chief. The Khorsabad inscription has that usurper say he besieged, took and occupied Samaria, carried into captivity twenty-seven thousand two hundred and eighty of its inhabitants, and set his own lieutenants over it; a damaged inscription elsewhere has him call himself conqueror of the far-off land of Judah. It was probably to this king, Ellicott concludes, that the words are addressed, and not to the successor commonly supposed before the inscriptions were read.

Matthew Henry keeps the older identification and frames both halves of the story. The destruction of the northern kingdom was foretold in the preceding chapter and accomplished in Hezekiah's sixth year, head and tail both cut off; the correction of Judah is foretold here and fell in his fourteenth, when a later Assyrian king, encouraged by his predecessor's success, took the fenced cities and besieged Jerusalem. It ended well, in the confusion of the Assyrians. The point Henry draws is the sovereignty in it: God deputed that king his servant and used him as a mere tool.

He alone turns the verse back on the people. Bad as they were, they appeared very good: a hypocritical nation professing religion and at that moment reformation, but not truly religious nor truly reformed, and not so good as they pretended now that a pious king had brought goodness into fashion. Gill puts the relation more plainly, that the Assyrian is called the rod of God's anger because he was used as an instrument to chastise Israel for their sins, and Wesley that God's anger against his people is what puts the weapons of war into Assyrian hands.

Clarke ends on the text rather than the history. The word standing for the staff itself seems to him to embarrass the sentence, and he omits it on the authority of the Alexandrian Greek and ten manuscripts, reading his staff instead; an archbishop, he reports, was likewise dissatisfied and proposed a different remedy, changing one word so the clause runs that he is a staff in the day of mine indignation.
6:
The commission is a single act to most, a standing rule to one. Charles Ellicott notes that the verb will bear I will send, I did send, or I am wont to send, and prefers the last: not a fact in history nor an isolated prediction but a law of the divine government. He would render the nation impious rather than hypocritical, and thinks the words for spoil and treading down carry a memory of Samaria's fall, walls pulled down, palaces turned to rubbish. John Gill keeps the received word, every one a hypocrite who served the Lord outwardly only. John Calvin makes the charge structural: since uprightness is the chief of the virtues, hypocrisy is the mother of all the vices, and the Lord's rod, like a father's, has a fixed destination.

What the instrument intended is the hinge. Keil and Delitzsch put it compactly: Asshur was to be an instrument of divine wrath upon Israel, but would exalt itself and make itself the end instead of the means. Gill spells it out: the Assyrian never imagined he was the rod of another's anger but thought himself his own master, and meant not to chastise the Jews but to destroy them and many nations. John Wesley adds why the point stands here: it justifies the judgments afterwards threatened against the Assyrian, who designed not God's will but the enlarging of his empire. Calvin turns it pastorally: when wicked men vomit out their rage they disturb weak minds, as though God could not restrain them, so the prophet steps forward beforehand.

Ellicott's contribution is documentary. The thoughts the prophet puts into the Assyrian's mouth match the egotism of the inscriptions, where I conquered, I besieged, I burnt, I killed, I destroyed is the recurring burden, mingled with the boast of championing Assyria's great deities. Behind the boast about the princes he sets the fact that one Assyrian king lists twenty-three who came to do homage at Damascus. Gill offers two readings, kings he had conquered and now ruled, or nobles whose wealth made them equal to kings.

The list of fallen cities is geography to one and psychology to the others. Ellicott says the six names point to recent conquests, one after another fallen, with the unspoken question whether Judah could escape. Calvin thinks they are cities or fortified places rather than countries, and hears the way wicked men talk proudly of what they have done so as to imagine nothing can stand in their way; blinded by pride, he adds, the Assyrian acknowledges no authority above his own, though none of us can move a finger without God's permission. Wesley reduces it to a taunt: he has conquered one place as well as another, the stronger as well as the weaker.

The last boast turns on a word its speaker would not have used. Ellicott observes that idols is hardly a term of scorn in an idolater's mouth, and supposes the prophet put into his lips the word he would himself have used; it is in character, though, for such a king to ascribe his victories to his own god as supreme, before whom local deities must bow, and to reckon the God of Israel one whose power was measured by the greatness of the nation worshipping him. Wesley reaches the same place from the other side: the speaker calls the gods of the nations, Jerusalem's not excepted, idols by way of contempt, judging them far inferior to the sun, the god of the Assyrians. Calvin says he insults not men only but God, and even the gods he himself worshipped, boasting that none could keep him from subduing their people. Both fix the moment: Gill cites a rabbi that what precedes was said before Samaria fell and this after, and Ellicott finds here the occasion of the utterance, the Assyrian threatening Jerusalem while campaigning on the Philistine coast.
12:
The boast breaks off here, and the break is marked variously. Charles Ellicott would read the opening word as a simple and rather than a wherefore: the proud king's speech is interrupted by the reassertion that he is only an instrument, and that when his work is done he too will be punished. John Calvin finds two clauses, that God will punish a wicked king and that the time is not yet come, and observes that wicked men act as though God were not in heaven. Keil and Delitzsch supply the mechanism: when God had punished to the point where he could go no further without destroying Israel, contrary to his mercy and truth, the punishing would turn against the instrument, which falls under the curse of all ungodly selfishness. John Wesley reads the whole work as the chastising of God's people for as long as he sees fit.

The fruit of the stout heart is where they part. Ellicott takes it to include all the words and acts in which the king's arrogance had shown itself. Adam Clarke would rather translate it the effect, following the Chaldee, which renders the word works.

On the boasting proper the readings run from grammar to divinity. Ellicott calls it another reproduction of the royal inscriptions' style, and identifies the practice behind one clause: merging independent nations into one empire was pursued more systematically by Assyria than by other conquerors, whose kings exulted in the title of remover of boundaries and landmarks. Calvin reads the strength as vast armies collected out of many nations, and says the prudence claimed is bestowed on tricks and dishonest cunning. John Gill turns it inward: if such arrogance in civil things is resented by God, much more in religious, when men ascribe salvation to their free will and the works of their hands.

The nest is the most vivid figure here, and Ellicott matches it from outside. An Assyrian inscription offers an almost verbal parallel, and in other documents the king is a colossal fowler for whom kingdoms are so many birds' nests to spoil and leave empty; the word rendered peeped means chirped, and not a fledgling was left in the nests he had despoiled. Calvin draws it from the other end: a man robbing a deserted nest takes the eggs easily, whereas if the parents were sitting they would fly at him and strike with the bill or drive him off with cries; the tyrant's boast is that not one ventured so much. Wesley notes the same, and calls the claim to have gathered all the riches of the earth a hyperbole not unusual in such mouths.

The answer to it is a question about tools. Gill marks where the speech ends and the prophet begins, deriding a boast as absurd as an axe ascribing the felling to itself and insisting the man who cut with it had no share. Calvin says the case is exactly that of an axe or saw despising the hand that sets it in motion and priding itself on an activity it has no power of its own to produce. Clarke works on the odd phrase that ends it, rendering it its master, and explains the idiom, a Hebrew way of joining the negative particle to a noun to express total absence of the thing named, as in help to the no-strength, the arm of the no-power, counsel to the no-wisdom. Ellicott hears in the figure what later Christian writers meant in calling a barbarian conqueror the scourge of God, and finds the comfort in it: the man's lust of power might be limitless, but God's compassion was the limit set to it. He would also render the clause as if the rod should shake them, taking the plural as generalising the comparison or, more probably, as pointing to God as the true wielder.
16:
The titles piled at the head of the sentence are deliberate. John Gill says they humble the boaster, Lord of greater armies than the Assyrian commanded. Keil and Delitzsch count three epithets designating God by his all-controlling omnipotence, one of which this prophet always uses of judicial manifestations. Adam Clarke notes that the glory under which the fire is kindled means all the king could boast of as strong in his forces.

The double figure that follows is famine and fire. Charles Ellicott makes the fat ones the army's warriors and says the fire burning the king's glory is explained next as the wrath of God. John Calvin reads both as the wealth and forces the king trusted in, and defends the first because prosperity is commonly likened to fatness, horses grown too fat becoming refractory. John Wesley has him stripped of wealth and might, his army destroyed as fire destroys combustible things cast into it.

That the same God is light to one people and fire to another is dwelt on by all. Gill has the Lord who calls his own out of darkness stand as a consuming fire to everyone else. Calvin puts it as physics: in fire are two things, light and heat, and the same power works contrary effects, shining on the godly to give them life while it consumes the ungodly. Delitzsch makes the two one, God being both fire and light, the former resolved in his self-life into the latter, so the word for holy stands parallel to that for light, God's being holy and his being pure light coming to one thing.

The thorns and the forest are sorted into ranks. Clarke takes the briers and thorns for the common people and the glory of the forest for the nobles, the fire destroying both, so the few who escape look like brands plucked from the burning. Ellicott divides them the same way, the thorns the host and the glory of the forest the captains, and finds the emphatic in one day pointing to a single catastrophe such as the one that afterwards destroyed that army. Gill allows the glory of the forest to mean the chief officers or the plunder taken from Egypt. Delitzsch reads the pair as a human forest and park, forest because the army came from many nations, garden ground because it boasted the beauty of men and armour.

Calvin denies the second word is a proper name and takes it for an appellative meaning rich soil, since the mountain of that name could not be said to belong to Assyria. On the eighteenth verse's last clause Ellicott reports that our version gives the extremity of exhaustion, the standard-bearer being chosen for strength and stature, so his giving way left no hope for the rest; but he judges the truer rendering to be that a sick man pines away, Delitzsch renders it the same way, as when a sick man dies, while Wesley keeps the received sense, a fallen standard-bearer striking panic into a whole army.

How few survived is answered three ways. Gill reports the rabbinic tradition that no more than ten escaped with their king, and a stricter version putting it at five, named. Ellicott observes that numbering a host and counting the killed was the royal scribe's work, often so shown in the Assyrian sculptures, and says the survivors are so few that a boy who could count only on his fingers would be skilled enough. Calvin makes the point from the other end, that children can barely count beyond three or four, and reads the clause as a Hebrew idiom for a number easily told: the Assyrian kingdom had been a vast forest, and when the trees are hewn down those left are few and scattered.
20:
The turn to the remnant is the point of the whole judgment. Matthew Henry recalls that the Lord was to perform his whole work upon Zion, and finds here what it is: the conversion of some, to whom the providence is sanctified and yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness though for the present grievous, and these only a remnant beside a people once as the sea sand. John Calvin puts the same lesson as consolation: because it is painful to endure calamities, the Lord shows us their result, that we may consider their design and bear them more patiently. You would wish the Assyrians driven off, he imagines God saying, but this chastisement is as necessary as medicine.

Charles Ellicott notes what the promise does not cover: for Assyria's remnant there is as yet no word of hope. For Israel's the prophet falls back on the thought in his own son's name, and Ellicott identifies the smiter they will lean on no longer as the Assyrian king whose protection an earlier king had courted instead of trusting the Holy One of Israel, the failure of that policy teaching them that faith was the truest wisdom. John Wesley confines it to such Jews as were preserved from the Assyrian scourge.

Whom the remnant returns to is the most consequential dispute. Adam Clarke says flatly that the mighty God is the Messiah, named in the preceding chapter. Keil and Delitzsch press it further: the title is God as historically manifested in the heir of David, and where another prophet sets the Lord and the second David side by side, this one sees them as one, so in New Testament language it would be to God in Christ. Ellicott finds the Immanuel promise behind the form of the words, and thinks the title must have reminded men of the Child who was to bear it. Gill and Calvin hear the allusion to the son's name as a pledge of deliverance without pressing the identification; Gill allows a return from captivity, a return to God by repentance, or, as he prefers, a turning to Christ.

The severity in the word remnant is not missed. Ellicott says it has that aspect as well as promise, since the hypocrites are not to expect they will escape punishment, the restoration being for the remnant only, and he notes the apostle's use of the passage. Calvin strikes at those who reckoned it enough to be Abraham's descendants after the flesh, then comforts the godly, so the shrinking of their number should not take them unawares.

The overflowing is where they disagree most sharply, and one doubts the word. Clarke observes that neither the Greek version, nor the apostle who follows it closely, nor any ancient version notices the word rendered overflowing, which seems to him to give an idea not easily reconciled with the words it stands among; he passes on a conjecture that its last two letters have been transposed and the true reading is judging, with strict justice. Ellicott keeps the received word and renders the clause a finished and decisive work overflowing with righteousness, punitive and corrective at once. Wesley keeps it, taking the destruction as decreed by God's fixed counsel and certain to be executed, overflowing them like a deluge, with justice and yet clemency, since a remnant was spared where all might have perished.

What the consumption is divides Gill from the rest. He denies it means the destruction of Judea and makes it the accomplishing of an absolute decree concerning the remnant's salvation, the decree of election, standing not upon works but upon God's sovereign will, so their salvation is sure. Delitzsch reads it to that end: in these more inward addresses the prophet means not to threaten but to comfort, and turns to the part of the nation that both needs consolation and can receive it.
24:
The comfort here is for some and not all. Matthew Henry notes that the prophet distinguishes the precious from the vile because providence does, speaking terror in the invasion to the hypocrites who were the people of God's wrath and comfort to the sincere who were the people of his love: the judgment came for the first, the deliverance for the second. John Calvin adds why it was necessary: many gloried in God's name while few performed what they professed, and after the kingdom's fall the godly might have judged their own case by the case of others. Charles Ellicott draws the practical conclusion, that the people should not give way to panic as in an earlier reign but abide the Assyrian march with the tranquillity of faith.

The phrase about Egypt is heard as threat and promise at once. Adam Clarke thinks the ambiguity designed: the Assyrian lifts his rod on the march up from Egypt, threatening God's people as Pharaoh had when he pursued them to the sea, but God in his turn will lift his rod over the sea as he did then, and the imitator of the Egyptians meets their end. Ellicott finds the ground of hope inside the phrase, since Pharaoh's cruelty was followed by the exodus, and quotes the Jewish proverb that when the tale of bricks is doubled deliverance is near. John Wesley reads it plainly, as the Egyptians formerly did.

How soon the very little while would run out is disputed. John Gill makes it a few days, the Assyrian army being destroyed by an angel shortly after it came against Jerusalem. Keil and Delitzsch caution that the expression does not date from the actual present. Calvin extends the horizon much further, holding that the prophet means not only the siege but the later calamities, the overthrow of the city, the razing of the temple and the carrying away of the inhabitants; commentators who neglect this, he says, cannot make the statements agree. Wesley takes the indignation as ceasing when vengeance is fully executed, Ellicott as the wrath poured out on God's people, which ceases so his anger may turn to their enemies' destruction.

Ellicott observes that in the old history the names stand at once for the Midianite chiefs and the places where they fell. Calvin notes that the prophet says scourge rather than rod, meaning the Lord will treat the enemies more harshly than they treated the Jews. Ellicott makes that repetition the turning point: the formula taken as an evil omen a few verses earlier returns as an augury of good, there having been another rod in the Egyptian story besides the oppressor's.

The last verse is the crux, and no one is satisfied with the received English. Ellicott calls it scarcely intelligible, though it suggests that the anointing marked out Judah's kings and priests as a consecrated people whose remembrance would move God to free them; most commentators, he reports, render it by reason of the fat, the figure being a bullock grown too fat for the yoke to go round his neck, a people waxing strong and asserting its freedom. Clarke follows a bishop who abandons the clause altogether, adopting the Greek reading from your shoulders because no good sense could be made of the present text, and adds an archbishop's conjecture, equally at a loss, of reading sons of oil, understood of the Jews as God's anointed. Wesley keeps the anointing and refers it to David, for whose sake God gave deliverances to later ages, and principally to the Messiah, of whom David was a type. Gill keeps to the historical burden, the tribute imposed on Hezekiah. Calvin declines to fix the deliverance to one event: most take it of the overthrow of the besieging army, which the march described next supports, and with that he partly agrees, but extends the prediction further.
28:
The march is admired as writing before it is read as geography. Keil and Delitzsch call it, aesthetically considered, one of the most magnificent descriptions human poetry has produced. Adam Clarke says the terror spreading through the places as the army advances is expressed with great brevity but finely diversified, and fixes the ground, all near Jerusalem, from the first town northward to the last westward. John Calvin explains why the itinerary is given: it sets the march before their eyes so the godly may stand firm, showing that the Assyrians did not move a step but by God's appointment. John Wesley notes that the prophet describes the invasion as present, the baggage left so the march may be faster.

Charles Ellicott marks a clean break here, the new section joined to what precedes only by subject; an inscription in which the Assyrian calls himself subduer of the lands of Judah puts the invasion beyond doubt.

The passage they cross is disputed. Clarke identifies the strait of Michmash, a narrow way between two hills where a great army might have been opposed by a far smaller one. Calvin doubts the view that the Jordan is meant, adopts the same strait, and draws the inference the others leave unstated: that the enemy passed unopposed shows all thought of a stand in open country was given up and the only resource left was the city's strength. Wesley says simply that the people fled to Jerusalem for fear.

The cry of the towns produces the prettiest philology here. Clarke follows the Syriac and renders the clause hearken unto her and answer her, holding that the prophet plays on the place-name, with peculiar propriety if it took that name from an echo; a lexicon he quotes gives the name the sense of responses, on the same principle as another meaning place of echo. Gill notes that the word for the cry serves also for a joyful sound and for the neighing of horses. Calvin takes it for howling heard at a distance, so loud that neighbouring cities catch the groaning, and observes that Hebrew calls cities daughters, which Wesley puts as a mother city and her lesser towns. Gill has one town's inhabitants removing on the news, and Calvin reads that verse as exaggerated speech, the place shaken as though carried bodily elsewhere, referring it to a people's disorderly flight.

The halt before the city is timed two ways. Gill has the invader arrive and stop short, staying briefly to prepare his army for the next day's march, and reports the Jewish tradition that he performed all his journeys in one day. Calvin knows the reading that he merely remains at a village next to Jerusalem, but agrees rather with those who make him halt with much of the day still before him to prepare the siege, the point being the march's speed and how near the city came to destruction.

The felling that ends the chapter changes the tone. Ellicott hears another pressure of the strong hand of God, the prophet telling the invader he shall come so far and no farther, and notes that the boughs and thickets repeat the earlier imagery, with the edge that Assyrian kings boasted of cutting down the forests of the nations they conquered. Gill takes the bough for the king and his army cut off in terrible manner, the word meaning a tree's ornament and glory; Wesley makes it the top bough and names the king. Clarke reports that many manuscripts, four editions and three versions read the word not as bough but as wine-press. On the closing clause some translate that the high cedars shall fall, but two commentators take the mighty one for the angel who smote the army, and Clarke holds that the Assyrian king is the one overthrown. Gill agrees, making the iron an angel excelling in strength.
